prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "RTX Corp" (ticker RTX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "RTX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: RTX Corporation
markets: Commercial aircraft engines and aftermarket (Pratt & Whitney)
Aircraft systems, avionics, interiors and aftermarket (Collins Aerospace)
Military engines (F135 for the F-35, F119)
Missiles and munitions (Tomahawk, SM-6, AMRAAM, Javelin with Lockheed, StormBreaker)
Air and missile defense radars and systems (Patriot, LTAMDS, SPY-6)
Space, sensors, electronic warfare and C5ISR

mission.plain: Use cutting-edge science to build the planes' parts, engines and defense systems that connect people and keep countries safe.

about.plain: RTX makes jet engines, airplane parts and weapons. Its Pratt & Whitney unit builds engines for airliners and fighter jets, Collins Aerospace makes things like cockpit electronics, seats and brakes, and Raytheon makes missiles, radars and defense systems. Airlines keep buying spare parts and repairs for decades after a plane is built, which brings in steady money.
about.customers: Airlines, plane makers like Airbus and Boeing, the US military and allied governments around the world.
about.everyday: If you have flown on an Airbus A320neo or many other airliners, there is a good chance RTX made the engine, the cockpit screens or the seats.

money.plain: jet engines for airliners and fighter jets, plus repairs and spare parts
airplane electronics, cabins, power and controls, plus spare parts
missiles, radars and air defense systems for governments
the GTF Advantage engine and hybrid-electric demonstrators for future, more efficient planes
cheap interceptors and lasers/microwaves that knock down drones

result.summary: RTX has a durable competitive advantage built on huge installed bases (the GTF and V2500 on narrowbodies, PW100 turboprops, F135 on every F-35, Patriot in 19-plus countries) that generate decades of high-margin aftermarket and sustainment revenue, plus regulatory certification and security-clearance barriers rivals cannot quickly copy. The moat is real but not flawless: the GTF powder-metal recall, fixed-price defense program charges and a 20% gross margin show limits to its pricing power, and its key franchises face strong peers such as CFM (GE/Safran) and Lockheed Martin.

pricingPower.evidence: Commercial aftermarket spare-part prices rise annually above inflation and backlog reached a record $289B at Q2 2026 (up from $268B at end-2025), yet consolidated gross margin is only about 20% (FY2025: $17,789M gross profit on $88,603M sales) because defense pricing is negotiated with the US government and fixed-price contracts and GTF compensation to airlines have caused large charges.

moats.evidence: Pratt & Whitney, Collins and Raytheon are century-old trusted names with thousands of patents and FAA/EASA type certificates, but buyers choose on certified performance and contracts rather than consumer brand.

Once an engine or avionics suite is certified on an aircraft, the airline or air force is locked into the OEM's parts and services for 25-30+ years, and Patriot users depend on Raytheon for upgrades, interceptors and sustainment.
There is a mild interoperability effect as allies standardize on Patriot and NATO-common munitions, but no true user network effect.
With $88.6B of 2025 sales and $2.8B of company-funded R&D, RTX can afford multi-decade engine and missile programs few rivals can, though its margins trail several peers.
Markets like large commercial engines (essentially CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce, GE) and US missile production support only a handful of suppliers, and the F135 is the sole engine for the F-35.
RTX is the incumbent; newer entrants like Anduril are counter-positioning against it with low-cost, software-led weapons.
Geared turbofan design, hot-section metallurgy, missile seekers and GaN radar manufacturing take decades of accumulated know-how and qualified supply chains to replicate.
Classified programs, export licenses, security-cleared engineers and sole-source positions (F135, Tomahawk, SM-6, Patriot) are hard for competitors to access.

customers.evidence: Customers keep re-ordering (record $289B backlog at Q2 2026, a seven-year $22.9B Tomahawk award in August 2026 and repeat Patriot buys by allies), but airlines have been angered by GTF groundings from the powder-metal inspections that required RTX to pay customer compensation.

talent.evidence: With more than 185,000 employees RTX is a top destination for aerospace engineers and security-cleared staff, but it is not a fixture of top 'best places to work' lists and competes for engineers with tech firms and higher-paying startups.

product.evidence: Its products are often the reference standard: Patriot is the most combat-proven Western air-defense system (including against ballistic missiles in Ukraine), the F135 powers every F-35, SPY-6 is the US Navy's new radar, and the GTF delivers about 16-20% better fuel burn than prior-generation engines, though its durability problems dent its reputation.

competitors.name: GE Aerospace (with Safran via CFM International)
competitors.note: CFM LEAP-1A competes head-on with the P&W GTF on the A320neo; GE also competes in military engines and engine aftermarket.

competitors.name: Lockheed Martin
competitors.note: Missiles and missile defense (PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, PrSM, JASSM) and hypersonics; also a partner on Javelin and the F-35.

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman
competitors.note: Sensors, radars, electronic warfare, space, solid rocket motors and missile defense (IBCS).

competitors.name: L3Harris Technologies
competitors.note: Electronic warfare, communications, space sensors and (via Aerojet Rocketdyne) rocket motors.

competitors.name: Safran
competitors.note: CFM engine partner, plus landing gear, seats, cabins, actuation and power systems against Collins.

competitors.name: Honeywell (Aerospace)
competitors.note: Avionics, APUs, engines for business jets and helicopters, and aftermarket services against Collins and P&W Canada.

competitors.name: Rolls-Royce Holdings
competitors.note: Widebody and business-jet engines and military engines; P&W partner via IAE on the V2500.

competitors.name: BAE Systems
competitors.note: Electronic warfare, munitions, sensors and combat systems in the US and Europe.

competitors.name: MBDA
competitors.note: European missile maker (owned by Airbus, BAE and Leonardo) competing for allied missile and air-defense orders, e.g. SAMP/T vs Patriot.

competitors.name: Thales
competitors.note: Avionics, in-flight entertainment, radars and air defense.

competitors.name: Boeing
competitors.note: Both customer and competitor: Boeing Defense in missiles, space and some systems; Boeing Global Services in aftermarket.

competitors.name: General Dynamics
competitors.note: Mission systems and C4ISR for the US government.

competitors.name: Anduril Industries
competitors.note: Venture-backed challenger in counter-drone systems, low-cost interceptors and autonomous weapons.

competitors.name: Kongsberg Gruppen
competitors.note: NASAMS air defense (co-developed with Raytheon) and Naval Strike Missile; partner and competitor.

competitors.name: TransDigm Group
competitors.note: Proprietary aerospace components competing with Collins in some parts and aftermarket.

estimates.name: GE Aerospace (with Safran via CFM International)
Rolls-Royce Holdings (estimate; not an SEC filer)
BAE Systems (estimate; not an SEC filer)
Kongsberg Gruppen (estimate; not an SEC filer)

threats: GTF powder-metal inspections keep hundreds of A320neo-family aircraft grounded, driving airline compensation costs and pushing customers toward the CFM LEAP.
Fixed-price defense development and production contracts can produce large charges when costs overrun.
Dependence on US defense budgets and foreign military sales, which can shift with politics, continuing resolutions and export-policy changes.
Low-cost, software-led challengers (Anduril and others) competing in drones, counter-drone and affordable munitions.
Supply-chain and labor constraints (castings, forgings, rocket motors, strikes) limiting output.
Tariffs on aerospace parts and materials, and legal/compliance exposure (the 2024 settlements over Middle East bribery and defective pricing).

ceo.name: Christopher T. Calio
ceo.background: Trinity College bachelor's degree, JD and MBA from the University of Connecticut; joined UTC in 2005, former president of Pratt & Whitney and RTX COO; chairman since 2025.

c1.evidence: Aerospace and defense is a large, mature industry growing mid-to-high single digits, and RTX is one of its leaders rather than the leader of a fast-emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers pick RTX for certified, combat-proven products (Patriot, F135, SM-6, GTF fuel efficiency) and 25-30-year support, which are hard to copy, though rivals like CFM and Lockheed offer close alternatives.

c3.evidence: Raytheon and Pratt & Whitney are well-known names and leaders in missiles and engines, but RTX is not a household default brand like Google or NVIDIA and GTF groundings have hurt airline goodwill.

c4.evidence: RTX talks about 'connecting and protecting our world' and pushing the boundaries of science, but management communication centers on execution, margins, free cash flow and backlog rather than an inspiring mission.

c6.evidence: “defense contractor, missiles, jet engines” — impressions are mixed: respected for engineering and national security, but associated with weapons and controversy over arms sales.

c7.evidence: Its markets are large (global defense budgets rising after the Ukraine war and Middle East conflicts; commercial air traffic growing ~4-5% a year) but are steady rather than secular hyper-growth.

c8.evidence: It can expand into counter-drone systems, hypersonics, space sensors, directed energy and hybrid-electric propulsion, but these are extensions of existing businesses rather than big new markets.

m1.evidence: Calio has a clear operational plan (three-segment structure, capacity investment, digital manufacturing) but is seen as an executor rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Calio is a professional manager who rose through UTC from 2005, not a founder, and runs the company with typical large-company priorities.

m4.evidence: He emphasizes customer delivery and safety (e.g. the GTF fleet management plan), but there is little distinctive evidence of servant leadership.

m5.evidence: RTX has a strong engineering culture and the CORE operating system for continuous improvement, but it is a merger of legacy cultures (UTC and Raytheon) rather than one deliberately built for invention.

m6.evidence: Calio has a law and business background (JD, MBA) rather than engineering, though he ran Pratt & Whitney and is close to its programs.

m7.evidence: There is no public controversy about Calio's character, but nothing distinctive shows a purpose beyond running a large defense contractor well.

m7b.evidence: No record of Calio giving a commencement speech at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Calio keeps a low public profile with a conventional executive style.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2024, sales rose from $68,920M (2023) to $88,603M (2025), adjusted EPS guidance was raised twice in 2026 to $7.10-7.25, and backlog hit a record $289B.

m10.evidence: RTX is not known for frugality; it is a large conglomerate-style contractor with typical big-company cost structures, though it runs cost-reduction programs.

c10.evidence: Its engines and avionics help billions of people fly each year, and its air defenses protect civilians from missiles, but its weapons are not a product that improves daily lives like Netflix or Google.

p2.evidence: Building jet engines, hypersonic and guided missiles, and radars that detect ballistic missiles is among the hardest engineering in the world and critical to air travel and national security.

f2.evidence: Operating margin went from a 2020 loss to 7.7% (2021), 8.2% (2022), 5.2% (2023, GTF charge), 8.1% (2024) and 10.5% (2025); improving overall but uneven.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $37,383M vs cash of $8,305M (about 4.7x FY2025 free cash flow of $7,940M), with positive equity of $68,116M.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $4,334M (2020) to $10,567M (2025) and operating profit from a loss to $9,300M, but both dipped in some years (2023 operating profit, 2024 cash flow).

v1.evidence: Some products are clearly best-in-class (Patriot, F135 as the only F-35 engine, SM-6), but its main commercial engine, the GTF, has had durability problems versus the rival LEAP.

v2.evidence: RTX is a sought-after employer for aerospace engineers and recent graduates, but it does not regularly appear near the top of employer rankings such as Glassdoor's Best Places to Work.

c5.evidence: If RTX vanished, airlines would lose engines and parts for thousands of aircraft and the US and allies would lose Patriot, Tomahawk and F-35 engines, though many people view weapons makers as morally mixed.
